newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: UN to award $610 mln to Kuwait for oil fire cost.
newsitem.headline: UN to award $610 mln to Kuwait for oil fire cost.

text.p: U.N. Security Council members were expected to approve a payment of $610 million to Kuwait Oil Company (KOC) on Tuesday for the cost of extinguishing fires in 800 oil wells set alight during the Gulf War, diplomats said.
Egypt, which raised technical queries on the award at the U.N. Compensation Commission (UNCC) on Monday, seemed ready to accept a decision, they added.
"We are still working on compromise language in the decision, but we are very close," an Arab diplomat said.
A Western diplomat, who asked not to be identified, said: "The bottom line is it is going to be all right."
KOC, a subsidiary of Kuwait Petroleum Corporation, filed its "well-blow out" claim for $950 million in July 1993.

A panel of three international arbitrators, named by the Gulf War reparations fund, recommended that Kuwait be awarded $610 million while $337 million be considered under another claim category, that of physical losses.

The UNCC's Governing Council, comprising representatives of the Security Council's 15 member-states, met informally to try to hammer out a consensus. A formal meeting to approve the report was scheduled for 1500 GMT.
It will be the first corporate claim approved by the Geneva-based body set up by the Security Council in 1991 to compensate damages caused during Iraq's invasion and seven-month occupation of Kuwait.

KOC alleged that Iraqi troops, fleeing Western and Arab forces led by the United States, had blown up 800 oil wellheads during the Gulf War. Twenty-seven firefighting teams from 10 countries including the United States and Kuwait, took months to extinguish the fires.
Dr. Adel Asem, deputy chairman of Kuwait's Public Authority for assessment of compensation for damages resulting from the Iraqi aggression, addressed the closed-door meeting on Monday.

"We hope that other oil sector claims will be reviewed in the near future, as the losses suffered by Kuwait's oil resources and industries, which are the main governmental productions, were among the most notorious and injurious of all losses suffered as a result of the Iraqi aggression," Asem said.
Iraq has denied responsibility for the oil-well fires, saying that the fires were caused by allied bombing.
The panel, chaired by Allan Philip of Denmark, was named in March 1995 to evaluate the KOC claim which was given priority.
A summary of the judges' report, obtained by Reuters, said:

"Based on the evidence and testimony presented, the panel finds that, although part of the damage for which compensation is being sought in the well blow-out claim may be a result of the allied bombing, the bulk of the oil-well fires were directly caused by the explosives placed on the wellheads and detonated by Iraqi armed forces.

"The evidence referred to by Iraq is consistent with this conclusion," it said. Under previous UNCC decisions, "Iraq's liability includes any loss suffered as a result of military operations by either side.
"Iraq's contention that the allied air raids broke the chain of causation therefore cannot be held," the judges said.
Egypt raised technical questions, while France warned against rushing a decision on huge sums, according to diplomats. China, Indonesia and Russia also sought clarifications.
"It is difficult because it is political. But I wouldn't say anyone was really objecting," said one developing country envoy.
"This is not a mailbox. After all, it is the Security Council," said another delegate. "This must be taken seriously."
Carlos Alzamora, executive-secretary of the Commission, is due to give a final press conference later in the day.
